title: AI Tools for Everyday Work: ChatGPT & More
tagline: Use ChatGPT and other AI assistants to write, study and work faster, with the checks that keep your facts right and your data safe.
takeaways: Keep private data out of AI
description:
AI chat tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot and Claude can draft an e-mail in seconds, explain a hard topic simply or help you plan a report. They can also invent a fact, add a job you never had or leak private data if you use them carelessly. This course teaches you to use them well, in simple steps, with examples from everyday life in Pakistan.

**Basic stages (free):**
- What AI chat tools are and how they work, in plain words, and how to start safely.
- First prompts: task, context, details and format, plus follow-ups that fix weak answers.
- Everyday uses: e-mails, CVs, summaries, Urdu and English translation and study, with fact-checking and privacy habits.

**Advanced stages (Premium):**
- Prompt frameworks, examples, chaining and iterating like a professional.
- AI for work outputs: reports, spreadsheet formulas, presentations and images, each with verification.
- Repeatable team workflows built on data privacy, fairness, copyright and company policy.

The skills work with any assistant. Plans and features change, so we teach skills, not buttons.

Fresh graduates and job seekers preparing CVs, cover letters and interviews
Small-business owners who write messages, posts and product descriptions every week
Office staff who produce e-mails, reports, spreadsheets and presentations
Anyone curious about ChatGPT who wants a safe, practical start

sessions.title: What AI Chat Tools Are and How They Work
sessions.summary: Meet ChatGPT and other AI assistants such as Gemini, Copilot and Claude. Learn in plain words how they produce answers, why they can be confidently wrong, and how to start safely through official apps.
objectives: Explain in plain words how an AI chat assistant produces an answer
Name ChatGPT and other common assistants and describe what they have in common
Recognise hallucinations and knowledge limits and know when to check
Choose between a search engine and an AI chat tool for a task
Start using an AI tool safely and avoid fake apps and scam offers

cards.title: Ayesha meets the talking computer
cards.setting: A small café near the university in Lahore. Evening. Ayesha has an assignment due and her cousin Bilal has his phone out.

lines.text: Welcome to the Smart Helper Trail. Over six stages you will learn to use AI chat tools well, safely and honestly. It starts with a cup of chai.
Everyone in my class talks about ChatGPT. Some say it does your homework. Some say it lies. I am honestly a bit scared to try it.
I used it yesterday for a cover letter. It wrote one in ten seconds! But it said I had three years of experience. I have zero.
That is the perfect start. These tools are very good with words and very confident, even when they are wrong. Both things are true.
Before you trust it or fear it, let us understand what it actually is. Then you can decide how to use it.
Okay. Teach me like I am a complete beginner, because I am.

cards.title: What an AI chat tool really does

scenes.heading: It learned from huge amounts of text
scenes.narration: An AI chat assistant is a computer program trained on a very large amount of written text. From this it learned patterns: which words usually follow which, how answers are shaped, how a polite e-mail sounds.

scenes.heading: It predicts the next words
scenes.narration: When you type a message, the tool works out a likely reply one small piece at a time. It is a very skilled word predictor. It does not look up a single true answer the way a dictionary does.

scenes.heading: It keeps the conversation in view
scenes.narration: Inside one chat, it can see what you said earlier. That is why a follow-up like 'make it shorter' works. A new chat usually starts fresh, unless the tool has a memory setting turned on.

scenes.heading: It can be confidently wrong
scenes.narration: Because it predicts plausible words, it can invent a fact, a name or a reference that sounds real. People call this a 'hallucination'. It is why you always check anything important.

scenes.heading: You are still in charge
scenes.narration: The tool gives you a draft or an explanation. You decide what is true, what fits your situation and what you send. Think of it as a fast helper, not a boss or a teacher who is always right.

cards.title: From your question to its answer
cards.caption: Every reply follows the same simple journey. Your part comes at the start and at the end.

items.label: You write a prompt
items.detail: A question or instruction, typed or spoken, in English, Urdu or Roman Urdu.

items.label: The tool reads the context
items.detail: Your message plus anything earlier in the same chat.

items.label: It predicts a reply
items.detail: It builds the answer piece by piece from patterns it learned.

items.label: You get a draft
items.detail: Fast, fluent and often helpful, but not guaranteed correct.

items.label: You check and decide
items.detail: Fact-check, edit and only then use it.

cards.question: Bilal's cover letter said he had three years of experience when he has none. What is the best explanation?
options: The tool searched the internet and found someone else's record by mistake
The tool is designed to exaggerate so that job applications look stronger
The tool predicted typical cover letter wording without knowing his real background
He was using a fake app, because real AI tools never make such mistakes
cards.explanation: AI chat tools produce likely-sounding text. Without his real details, it filled the gap with typical wording. Real, well-known tools also make such mistakes, which is why you check every claim.

cards.title: ChatGPT and the other assistants
cards.body:
**ChatGPT** is the best-known AI chat assistant, but it is not the only one. Other popular assistants include **Gemini**, **Copilot** and **Claude**, and new ones keep appearing.

- They all work in a similar way: you type, they reply in natural language.
- Each has its own strengths, style and settings, and they change often.
- Most offer some free use and paid plans. What is included **varies by plan, country and time**, so check the current terms on the official website before you rely on a feature.

The skills in this course work with any of them. Learn the skill, not the button.

cards.back: The message or instruction you give the AI tool. A clearer prompt usually gets a more useful answer.
The trained program behind the chat. Different tools use different models, and models are updated over time.
When the tool states something false or made-up in a confident way, such as a fake book title or a wrong date.
Much of what a model knows comes from data up to a certain date. It may not know recent events unless it can search the web.
The earlier messages in a conversation. The tool uses them to understand follow-up requests.
AI that creates new content, such as text, images or audio, instead of only sorting or labelling data.

cards.title: Search engine or AI chat?
cards.caption: Both are useful. They answer in different ways, so pick the right one for the job.

items.label: What you get
items.left: A list of links to real web pages
items.right: One written answer in its own words

items.label: Best for
items.left: Finding a specific source, shop or official page

items.label: Sources
items.left: You can see who published each page
items.right: Often no source unless you ask, and some tools cannot show one

items.label: Main risk
items.right: Fluent answers that may contain invented facts

items.label: Your job
items.right: Check facts against a trusted source

cards.title: Ayesha's first question
cards.situation: Ayesha wants to understand photosynthesis for her biology class tomorrow. She has her textbook, and she has just opened an AI chat tool for the first time. What should she do?

choices.text: Ask the AI to explain photosynthesis simply, then compare its explanation with her textbook chapter
choices.outcome: Excellent. The AI gives her a friendly explanation, and the textbook confirms the facts. If the two disagree, she trusts the textbook and asks her teacher.

choices.text: Ask the AI to explain it and memorise the answer word for word
choices.outcome: Risky. The explanation may be good, but it could contain a small mistake, and memorising exact AI wording does not build real understanding.

choices.text: Skip the AI and only read the textbook, because AI always lies
choices.outcome: Safe but limiting. AI is not always wrong; it can be a patient explainer. The skill is using it and checking it, not avoiding it completely.

cards.title: Good job for AI, or not?
cards.prompt: Sort each task by how well an AI chat tool suits it for a beginner.

items.text: Rewording a message to a teacher so it sounds polite
Getting ideas for a birthday party on a small budget
Explaining a hard topic in simpler words
Finding today's dollar-to-rupee rate
Getting the dose of a medicine for a child
Learning the facts of a recent news event
Deciding whether to sign a legal contract
Getting a list of famous Pakistani poets with dates

cards.question: Which statement about AI chat tools is most accurate?
options: They create answers from patterns, so even fluent answers need checking
They copy the single correct answer from a hidden database
They only give wrong answers when the question is in Urdu
They always show the exact source of every sentence they write
cards.explanation: AI chat tools generate text from patterns they learned. Fluency is not proof. They do not copy from one true database, and many answers come without sources.

cards.title: Match the assistant to the idea
cards.prompt: Match each phrase to what it means in plain words.

pairs.right: Names of different AI chat assistants that work in a similar way
Options that differ by tool and change over time, so check current terms
The safest place to download or open an AI tool
Usually starts without the earlier conversation in view

cards.title: Fake apps and scam messages
cards.body:
As AI became popular, so did scams using its name. Fictional example: Kamran in Peshawar got a WhatsApp message saying "ChatGPT Pro free for Pakistan, pay Rs 500 activation by JazzCash". He paid. Nothing happened, and the number stopped replying.

**Warning signs:**
- Offers sent by unknown numbers or pop-up ads.
- Payment through personal mobile wallet numbers.
- Apps with odd names, few reviews or a developer you do not recognise.
- Requests for your passwords or OTP codes.

**Safe habit:** open the tool through its official website, or download it from the official app store after checking the developer name carefully.

cards.title: Your safe first session
cards.prompt: Put these first steps with a new AI tool in a sensible order.
steps: Open the tool from its official website or official app store listing
Create an account with a strong password you do not use elsewhere
Read the short notes on privacy and data settings
Ask a simple, low-risk question to see how it replies
Check its answer against something you already know

cards.title: Start where you can judge the answer
cards.body: Your first prompts should be about things you already know a little. Ask it to explain something from your own field, summarise a text you have read, or reword your own message. When you know the topic, you can spot mistakes, and you quickly learn how far to trust it.

cards.question: Ayesha asks an AI tool about a cricket match played last night. It gives a confident score. What should she remember?
options: Scores from AI are always live and official, because AI is connected to the stadium
If the answer sounds confident and detailed, it must be correct
AI tools refuse all sports questions, so the score must be a joke
The tool may not have recent information, so she should check a reliable sports source
cards.explanation: Many models have a knowledge cut-off and some cannot search the web, or may search and still misread. For recent facts, check a trusted, up-to-date source.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Curious Café
items: An AI chat assistant is a trained program that predicts useful-sounding text; it is not a perfect fact machine.
ChatGPT is the best-known, and Gemini, Copilot and Claude are other examples; the skills in this course work with all of them.
Fluent and confident does not mean correct: check names, numbers, dates and facts that matter.
Plans and features vary by tool, country and time, so check the current terms on the official site.
Use only official apps and websites, and ignore offers that ask for wallet payments or OTP codes.

cards.prompt: Think of one small task this week where an AI tool could save you time. What would you ask it, and how would you check that its answer is right?

quiz.question: In plain words, how does an AI chat assistant produce its answer?
options: It phones a human expert who types the answer very quickly
It copies the single correct answer from one official encyclopaedia website that it keeps open
It predicts a likely reply from patterns learned from large amounts of text
It picks a random saved reply from a fixed list of answers
quiz.explanation: AI chat tools generate text by predicting likely words from patterns they learned during training. They do not call experts or copy from one source.

quiz.question: What does 'hallucination' mean when people talk about AI chat tools?
options: The tool states something false or invented as if it were true
The tool shows a colourful moving picture instead of a written answer, usually by accident
The tool stops replying because the internet is too slow
The tool refuses a question because it is against its rules
quiz.explanation: A hallucination is a confident but false or made-up statement, such as a fake reference or wrong date.

quiz.question: Which of these is NOT an AI chat assistant?
options: ChatGPT
Gemini
Claude
A calculator app that only adds and subtracts numbers
quiz.explanation: ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude are AI chat assistants (Copilot is another). A simple calculator follows fixed rules and does not generate language.

quiz.question: Bilal sees a WhatsApp message offering 'ChatGPT Pro free for Pakistan' if he sends Rs 500 to a mobile wallet number. What should he do?
options: Pay quickly before the offer ends, because popular AI tools often run special discounts for Pakistan
Ignore it and use only the official website or app store listing
Send the money but ask for a receipt on WhatsApp first
Forward it to friends so they can also get the free plan
quiz.explanation: Offers from unknown numbers asking for wallet payments are classic scam signs. Official tools are reached through their official website or verified app listing.

quiz.question: Why might an AI tool give a wrong answer about something that happened yesterday?
options: AI tools only work on weekdays and skip weekend news
Its training data may stop at an earlier date, so it may not know recent events
It deliberately hides recent news from users in Pakistan
Recent events are always too complicated for any computer program to describe correctly in words
quiz.explanation: Many models have a knowledge cut-off. Some can search the web, but you should still check recent facts with a reliable, current source.

quiz.question: Ayesha asks a follow-up, 'Now explain it in simpler words', and the tool understands. Why?
options: It reads her textbook through the phone camera without asking
It guesses, because every simple question has the same answer
Her teacher has linked her class notes to the AI tool
It can see the earlier messages in the same chat
quiz.explanation: Inside one conversation, the chat history gives the tool context for follow-up requests. A brand-new chat usually starts fresh.

quiz.question: What is the main difference between a search engine and an AI chat assistant?
options: A search engine lists pages to visit; an AI chat writes one answer in its own words
A search engine is always correct and checked by experts; an AI chat assistant is always wrong about facts
A search engine works only in English; AI chat works only in Urdu
There is no difference; they are two names for the same thing
quiz.explanation: Search engines point you to sources. AI chat tools generate a written answer, often without showing sources, so checking matters.

quiz.question: Where can you find what is included in a tool's free or paid plan?
options: In this course, because plans and prices are fixed for every tool, in every country, for every year
From any social media post that mentions the tool's name
On the tool's official website, because plans vary and change over time
From the AI itself, because it always knows its own latest prices
quiz.explanation: Plans differ by tool, country and time. The official website has the current terms; social media and the AI's own answers may be out of date.

quiz.question: Which first task is the safest way to learn how far to trust an AI tool?
options: Asking for medical advice for a family member's illness
Asking it to decide which university you should join
Asking it for the exact legal fee for registering a company
Asking about a topic you already know well, so you can spot mistakes
quiz.explanation: When you know the topic, you can judge the answer. High-stakes questions like medicine, law and fees need trusted human or official sources.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes your role when you use an AI chat tool?
options: You accept its reply, because a computer cannot make mistakes
You treat its reply as a draft and decide what is true and what to use
You copy its reply without reading it, to save as much time as possible
You let it decide for you whenever you feel unsure about something
quiz.explanation: AI gives drafts and explanations. You stay responsible for checking, editing and deciding.

sessions.title: First Prompts and Getting Useful Answers
sessions.summary: Turn vague questions into clear prompts using four simple ingredients: task, context, details and format. Practise follow-ups that fix tone, length and level, and write prompts in English, Urdu or Roman Urdu.
objectives: Write a prompt with a clear task, context, details and format
Use follow-up prompts to change length, tone and level
Ask the tool to ask you questions before it writes
Prompt in English, Urdu or Roman Urdu and choose the reply language
Decide when to restart with a new chat

cards.title: Bilal's one-line prompt
cards.setting: Bilal's room in Gulshan-e-Iqbal, Karachi. He has an interview next week and a laptop full of half-written notes.

lines.text: I typed 'interview tips' and got a long list. Make eye contact, dress well, be on time. My mother already told me all of this!
What job is the interview for, and what worries you most?
Junior accounts officer at a textile company. I get nervous when they ask about weaknesses, and I studied commerce, not textiles.
None of that was in your prompt. The tool gave a general answer because it got a general question.
So I should talk to it like I talk to you?
Exactly. Give it the situation, the task and what you want back. Let us build a better prompt together.

scenes.heading: Say the task clearly
scenes.narration: Start with what you want: write, explain, summarise, list, compare, correct. 'Give me five practice interview questions' is clearer than 'interview tips'.

scenes.heading: Give the context
scenes.narration: Tell it who you are and what the situation is. 'I am a fresh commerce graduate interviewing for a junior accounts officer job at a textile company in Karachi.'

scenes.heading: Add the details that matter
scenes.narration: Length, level, deadline, audience, anything to include or avoid. 'Keep each answer under 80 words. Avoid fancy words.'

scenes.heading: Ask for a format
scenes.narration: A table, bullet points, a short e-mail, three options. A format makes the answer easier to use straight away.

scenes.heading: Keep talking
scenes.narration: The first answer is a starting point. Reply with 'shorter', 'more formal', 'give two more examples' or 'ask me questions first'.

cards.title: Four ingredients of a good prompt
cards.caption: You do not need all four every time, but adding even one usually improves the answer.

items.label: Task
items.detail: What you want done, starting with an action word.

items.label: Context
items.detail: Who you are, who it is for and the situation.

items.label: Details
items.detail: Length, level, tone, must-haves and must-avoids.

items.label: Format
items.detail: Bullets, table, e-mail, steps or a set number of options.

items.label: Interview
items.right: Give me 5 likely questions for a junior accounts officer interview at a Karachi textile firm, with short sample answers

items.label: E-mail
items.right: Write a polite, short e-mail to my landlord asking to fix a water leak in the kitchen by Friday

items.label: Study
items.right: Explain inflation to a first-year student using an example with prices of roti and petrol, in under 150 words

items.label: Business
items.right: Write 3 short Facebook captions for my Faisalabad lawn suit shop's Eid sale, friendly tone, Roman Urdu and English mix

cards.question: Which prompt is most likely to get Bilal a useful answer?
options: 'Interview'
'Ask me 5 interview questions for a junior accounts job, one at a time, and give feedback on my answers'
'Tell me everything about every type of job interview in the world'
'Are interviews hard?'
cards.explanation: The best prompt gives a clear task, a context and a way of working (one at a time with feedback). The others are too vague or too broad.

cards.title: Name the ingredient
cards.prompt: Match each part of a prompt to the ingredient it adds.

pairs.right: Task

pairs.left: 'to my manager after my first week at a bank in Islamabad'
pairs.right: Context
Details

pairs.left: 'give me two versions to choose from'
pairs.right: Format

cards.title: Follow-up prompts: the real secret
cards.body:
Most good results come from a short conversation, not one perfect prompt. After the first answer, you can:

- **Shorten or expand:** 'Cut this to three lines.' 'Add one example.'
- **Change the tone:** 'Make it more formal.' 'Make it friendlier.'
- **Change the level:** 'Explain this to a 12-year-old.' 'Use accounting terms.'
- **Fix mistakes:** 'I have no work experience; remove that line.'
- **Ask it to ask you:** 'Before you write, ask me three questions about my background.'

If the chat goes badly off track, start a **new chat** with a clearer first prompt. That is often faster than fixing a muddled conversation.

cards.back: Use when the answer is too long to read or send. You can give a limit, such as 50 words.
Use when the task depends on your personal details, like a CV or a speech.
Use when you want to choose a style, a subject line or a caption.

cards.front: 'Explain like I am new to this'
cards.back: Use when the answer is full of words you do not know.
Use to see guesses the tool made, so you can correct them.
Use to compare things side by side, such as two phone packages.

cards.title: The answer is full of hard words
cards.situation: Ayesha asks an AI tool to explain supply and demand. The reply is accurate but full of terms like 'equilibrium' and 'elasticity'. She feels lost. What is her best next step?

choices.text: Reply: 'Explain this again for a beginner, using an example from a Lahore fruit market, and define any hard word'
choices.outcome: Great choice. A follow-up with a level and a local example usually produces a much clearer answer. She stays in the same chat so the tool keeps the topic.

choices.text: Close the app and decide that AI is only for clever people
choices.outcome: This throws away a useful helper. The tool was not wrong, it just aimed at the wrong level. One follow-up would have fixed it.

choices.text: Copy the hard answer into her notes and hope it makes sense later
choices.outcome: Her notes now contain words she does not understand. Asking for a simpler version first would help her learn.

cards.title: Improve a prompt step by step
cards.prompt: Put the steps for turning a weak first try into a strong result in order.
steps: Write a first prompt with the task you want done
Read the answer and notice what is missing or wrong
Add context and details you forgot to mention
Ask for the format you need, such as a list or e-mail
Check the final version yourself before you use it

cards.question: Nasreen wants Instagram captions for her boutique but the tool's first attempt sounds very formal. What should she do?
options: Delete her account and create a new one
Reply in the same chat: 'Make them friendly and short, like a local shop talking to regular customers'
Type the same first prompt again, word for word, and hope for change
Accept the formal captions because AI knows marketing better than her
cards.explanation: A follow-up with clear direction on tone is the quickest fix. Repeating the same prompt gives similar results, and she knows her customers best.

cards.title: Roman Urdu prompts work too
cards.body:
You do not have to write perfect English. Many assistants understand Urdu script and Roman Urdu, though quality can vary by tool and topic.

Fictional example, Nasreen's prompt:

> Meri lawn suits ki dukaan Faisalabad mein hai. Eid sale ke liye 3 chhote WhatsApp messages likho, friendly tone, English aur Urdu mix. Har message 40 words se kam.

The tool replied with three short messages. Nasreen changed one word in each so they sounded like her, then sent them.

**Tip:** say clearly which language and script you want back, for example 'Reply in Urdu script' or 'Reply in simple English'.

cards.title: Task, context, details or format?
cards.prompt: Sort each piece of a prompt into the ingredient it mainly adds.

items.text: 'Summarise this article'
'I run a small mobile repair shop in Peshawar'
'Under 100 words'
'Avoid technical terms'
'As five bullet points'
'In a two-column table'
'For my customers who are mostly elderly'
'Use a respectful tone'

cards.title: Give an example of what you like
cards.body: If you have a message or paragraph whose style you like, paste it (with any private details removed) and say 'write in a similar style'. One good example often explains your taste better than a long description.

cards.question: What is usually the best thing to do when a long chat has become confused and keeps repeating the same mistake?
options: Keep typing 'wrong' until the tool finally understands
Assume the tool is broken and never use it again
Add more and more unrelated questions to the same chat
Start a new chat with a clear first prompt that includes all the key details
cards.explanation: A fresh chat with a clear, complete prompt removes the confusing history. It is often faster than repairing a muddled conversation.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Prompt Bazaar
items: Vague prompts get general answers; give a clear task, the context, key details and a format.
The first answer is a starting point: use follow-ups to shorten, change tone, change level or fix errors.
Ask the tool to ask you questions first when the task depends on your personal details.
You can write in English, Urdu or Roman Urdu; say which language you want back.
If a chat goes off track, start a new chat with a better first prompt.

cards.prompt: Write down one vague question you have asked an AI tool or a search engine recently. Rewrite it using task, context, details and format. What do you expect to change in the answer?

quiz.question: What is a 'prompt'?
options: The reply that the AI tool sends back to you
A warning that appears when the internet is slow
The message or instruction you give an AI tool
The monthly bill for using a paid AI plan
quiz.explanation: A prompt is what you type or say to the tool. Its quality strongly shapes the answer.

quiz.question: Which part of this prompt is the context? 'Write a short leave request. I am a cashier at a pharmacy in Rawalpindi. Keep it formal.'
options: 'I am a cashier at a pharmacy in Rawalpindi'
'Write a short leave request'
'Keep it formal'
The word 'short' on its own
quiz.explanation: Context tells the tool who you are and the situation. 'Write a short leave request' is the task, and 'keep it formal' is a detail about tone.

quiz.question: Bilal typed 'interview tips' and got a very general answer. What was the main reason?
options: The tool does not know anything about job interviews
Interviews in Pakistan are too different for AI to understand
His prompt gave no task details, context or format
He should have typed the prompt in capital letters
quiz.explanation: A general prompt gives a general answer. Adding the job, his worries and the format he wants would give focused help.

quiz.question: Which follow-up is most useful when an answer uses words you do not understand?
options: 'Explain this again for a beginner and define any difficult words'
'This is wrong'
'Write the same thing again'
'Make it much longer and more detailed, and add more technical words so it sounds expert'
quiz.explanation: Asking for a beginner level and definitions directly fixes the problem. 'This is wrong' gives no direction.

quiz.question: When is 'Ask me three questions before you start' a smart instruction?
options: When you want a quick definition of a common word
When you want the tool to finish as fast as possible without input
When you are asking for a simple maths calculation
When the task depends on personal details, like writing your CV summary
quiz.explanation: Letting the tool ask questions first gathers the facts it needs, so it does not invent them. That is especially useful for personal documents.

quiz.question: Nasreen writes her prompt in Roman Urdu. What should she add to get the reply in the form she wants?
options: Nothing, because AI tools always reply in English only, whatever language or script the prompt is in
Say which language and script she wants back, for example 'reply in Urdu script'
A long apology for not writing in perfect English
A request for the tool to translate her shop's name
quiz.explanation: Many tools understand Roman Urdu, but stating the language and script for the reply avoids surprises.

quiz.question: Which of these adds a format to a prompt?
options: 'I am a second-year student'
'Give the answer as a table with two columns'
'Write about climate change'
'Make it sound friendly'
quiz.explanation: A format describes the shape of the answer, such as a table, list or e-mail. The others are context, task and tone.

quiz.question: A chat has gone in circles for 20 messages. What is usually the quickest fix?
options: Keep replying 'try again' until the answer changes
Switch the phone off and on again before typing anything
Paste the same confusing message three more times
Open a new chat and write a clear, complete first prompt
quiz.explanation: A fresh start with all key details removes the confusing history and usually gets a better answer quickly.

quiz.question: Why can pasting an example of a style you like improve the answer?
options: It shows the tool your preferred tone and length more clearly than a description
It lets the tool copy the text and avoid any work at all
It is required before any AI tool will reply to you
It makes the tool's answer automatically correct in every fact, because examples switch on a checking mode
quiz.explanation: An example communicates style quickly. Remove private details first, and remember that style is not the same as accuracy.

quiz.question: Which prompt is the clearest?
options: 'marketing'
'Tell me about business'
'List 5 low-cost marketing ideas for a small bakery in Hyderabad, in bullet points'
'Can you help me?'
quiz.explanation: It has a task (list ideas), context (small bakery in Hyderabad), a detail (low-cost, 5) and a format (bullets).

sessions.title: Everyday Uses: E-mails, CVs, Summaries, Translation and Study
sessions.summary: Use AI to write e-mails and CVs, summarise texts, translate between Urdu and English and study smarter, while building the two habits that keep you safe: fact-checking before you use anything and keeping private data out.
objectives: Draft e-mails, messages and CV wording with AI and edit them in your own voice
Summarise and translate Urdu and English texts and check the results
Use AI as an honest study partner within your institution's rules
Fact-check names, numbers, dates and prices against trusted sources
Keep personal, customer and confidential data out of AI tools

cards.title: Three jobs before lunch
cards.setting: A Saturday morning. Nasreen's boutique in Faisalabad, with Ayesha and Bilal visiting on a video call.

lines.text: I need an e-mail to a fabric supplier in Karachi, a price list in English and Urdu, and my nephew wants help with his CV. All before lunch!
And I want AI to fix my CV too. Last time it gave me a job I never had, remember?
I have a 20-page chapter to summarise for my exam. Can it do that?
Yes, AI can help with all of these. But each one needs a check at the end. A wrong price, a fake job or a missed point can cost you.
And can I paste my customers' phone numbers so it can write to each of them?
Good question, and the answer is no. Today we learn the everyday uses and the two habits that keep you safe: fact-checking and privacy.

cards.title: Everyday uses that save real time

scenes.heading: E-mails and messages
scenes.narration: Give the purpose, the reader and the tone. 'Polite e-mail to a supplier asking for a new delivery date, firm but friendly.' Then edit the draft so it sounds like you.

scenes.heading: CVs and cover letters
scenes.narration: Paste your real details and ask it to improve wording and layout. Never let it add experience, grades or skills you do not have. Employers do check.

scenes.heading: Summaries
scenes.narration: Paste a text and ask for the main points in bullets. For long documents, summarise a section at a time and compare with the original for missed points.

scenes.heading: Translating Urdu and English
scenes.narration: AI can translate quickly, but names, numbers, idioms and politeness need checking. For legal or official papers, use a qualified human translator.

scenes.heading: Studying
scenes.narration: Ask for simple explanations, examples and practice questions. Follow your school or university rules on AI, and do your own work for assessments.

cards.title: The draft, check, edit, send loop
cards.caption: Use this loop for every everyday task. The check step is never optional.

items.label: Draft with AI
items.detail: Get a first version quickly from a clear prompt.

items.label: Check facts
items.detail: Names, numbers, dates, prices and claims against a trusted source.

items.label: Edit in your voice
items.detail: Remove anything untrue or unlike you; add the personal touch.

items.label: Send or use
items.detail: Only when you would be happy to put your name on it.

cards.question: Bilal asks AI to improve his CV. It adds 'Advanced Excel certification'. He has used Excel but has no certificate. What should he do?
options: Remove the line and keep only skills and qualifications he can prove
Keep it, because AI knows what employers want to read
Keep it and plan to get the certificate after he is hired
Change it to 'expert in all software' so it sounds even stronger
cards.explanation: A CV must be truthful. Invented qualifications can be checked and can cost a job offer. Describe real skills honestly, such as 'used Excel for monthly sales reports'.

cards.title: Fact-checking in four quick moves
cards.body:
Before you use an AI answer that matters, run four quick checks:

1. **Spot the claims.** Underline every name, number, date, price, law or quote.
2. **Find a trusted source.** An official website, your textbook, a known newspaper, the supplier's own price list.
3. **Compare.** Does the source say the same thing? If not, trust the source.
4. **Ask the tool for its reasoning.** 'How did you get this number?' can reveal a guess. But never treat the tool as proof of itself.

The bigger the consequence, the stronger the check. A party idea needs none. A medicine, a fee or a deadline needs an official or professional source.

cards.title: Never paste these into an AI tool

cards.back: Identity numbers can be misused for fraud. Keep them out of AI chats completely.
No genuine tool or company needs these in a chat. Anyone asking for them is a red flag.
Account numbers, card numbers and PINs should never go into a chat tool.
Names with phone numbers, addresses or orders belong to your customers, not to a chat tool.
Health information is highly private. Remove names and details if you ask a general question.
Your employer's documents may be secret. Follow company policy before pasting anything.

cards.title: How much checking does it need?
cards.caption: Place the task by how much it matters if wrong and how easy it is to check. Top-right tasks need the strongest checks.

items.label: Easy to check, matters a lot
items.detail: A supplier e-mail with prices: check every number against your price list.

items.label: Hard to check, matters a lot
items.detail: Medical, legal or money advice: use official or professional sources.

items.label: Easy to check, matters little
items.detail: A birthday message: read it once and send.

items.label: Hard to check, matters little
items.detail: Fun facts for a chat with friends: fine, but do not repeat them as truth.

cards.title: Nasreen's customer list
cards.situation: Nasreen wants personal Eid messages for 200 regular customers. Her spreadsheet has each customer's full name, phone number, address and last order. She asks you how to use AI for this. What do you suggest?

choices.text: Ask AI for two or three warm message templates with a [Name] placeholder, then fill in names herself or with her messaging tool
choices.outcome: Best choice. She gets the time saving without giving any customer data to the AI tool. The personal touch comes from her own list.

choices.text: Paste the whole spreadsheet into the chat and ask for 200 personal messages
choices.outcome: This shares customers' private data with an outside tool, which they did not agree to. It may also break her bank or platform rules. Avoid it.

choices.text: Paste only names and last orders, but remove phone numbers and addresses
choices.outcome: Better than pasting everything, but still shares personal information about real people. Templates with placeholders do the job without any customer data.

cards.title: Safe to paste or not?
cards.prompt: Sort each item by whether it is safe to paste into a general AI chat tool.

items.text: A public news article you want summarised
Your own CV with your phone number and address
A customer complaint with the customer's name and order number
Your online banking password
A chapter from your own class notes
A photo of your CNIC
Your company's unreleased sales targets
A general question about how to price handmade jewellery

cards.question: Ayesha asks AI to translate a formal letter from Urdu to English for a visa application. What is the safest approach?
options: Submit the AI translation directly, because AI is perfect at Urdu
Translate only the first paragraph and leave the rest in Urdu
Use AI to understand it, then get an official or qualified translation for the application
Ask the AI to add extra details to make the application stronger
cards.explanation: For official documents, mistakes can have serious results. AI can help you understand, but official uses usually need a qualified translator and the exact requirements of the office concerned.

cards.title: Ayesha's honest study session
cards.body:
Ayesha has an economics exam in Islamabad next week. Fictional example of how she studies with AI:

- She reads her chapter first, then asks: 'Summarise the main points of this text in 8 bullets' and pastes her own notes.
- She compares the bullets with the chapter and finds one point missing, which she adds herself.
- She asks: 'Give me 10 practice multiple-choice questions on these points, with answers at the end.'
- She answers them on paper first, then checks.

What she does **not** do: submit AI-written work as her own. Her university's rules on AI apply, and the exam tests her, not the tool.

cards.title: Match the task to the best check
cards.prompt: Match each everyday task to the check it needs most.

pairs.right: Compare every price with your own price list
Ask a fluent speaker to read it for tone and errors
Skim the original for important points that were missed
Remove anything you did not actually do or achieve
Compare with your textbook or teacher's notes

cards.title: Remove details, keep the question
cards.body: You can often get the same help without private data. Replace names with [Customer], numbers with [Amount] and companies with [Supplier]. The tool can still write the message, and you fill in the real details yourself after.

cards.question: Which of these is the best use of AI for studying?
options: Asking AI to write an assignment and submitting it under your own name
Copying AI explanations into an exam answer sheet from your phone
Using AI answers only, without ever opening the course book
Asking for practice questions on a topic and checking your answers against the textbook
cards.explanation: AI is a great practice partner. Submitting its work as your own breaks most academic rules and skips the learning.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Everyday Market
items: AI can draft e-mails, improve CVs, summarise texts, translate and help you study, saving real time.
Use the draft, check, edit, send loop: never send or submit AI output without checking it.
Check names, numbers, dates and prices against trusted sources; the higher the stakes, the stronger the check.
Never paste CNIC numbers, passwords, bank details, customers' personal data or confidential work files.
Keep it honest: no invented CV experience, and follow your institution's rules on AI for coursework.

cards.prompt: Choose one real message, document or study task from your week. How would you use AI for it, what would you remove for privacy, and which check would you run before using the result?

quiz.question: In the draft, check, edit, send loop, which step must never be skipped?
options: Drafting the text by hand before asking AI
Sending the same message to everyone in your contacts
Asking the AI to rate its own answer out of ten
Checking the facts before you use the draft
quiz.explanation: Checking catches invented or wrong details before they reach anyone. The other options are not part of the loop.

quiz.question: Which item should never be pasted into a general AI chat tool?
options: A public article you want summarised
Your online banking password
A general question about writing a cover letter
Your own class notes on a history topic
quiz.explanation: Passwords should never be shared in any chat. Public articles, general questions and your own notes are normally fine.

quiz.question: Nasreen wants personalised messages for 200 customers. What is the most privacy-friendly method?
options: Paste her full customer spreadsheet so the AI can personalise each message
Paste names and phone numbers only, because addresses are the private part
Ask AI for templates with a [Name] placeholder and fill in names herself
Ask each customer to send their details to the AI tool directly
quiz.explanation: Templates with placeholders give the time saving with no customer data going into the tool.

quiz.question: An AI tool translates a shop poster into Urdu. What is the best check before printing it?
options: Ask a fluent Urdu reader to check the meaning, tone and spelling
Count the number of words to make sure it matches the English
Print it straight away, because AI translation is always accurate
Translate it back into English with a different tool and stop there
quiz.explanation: A fluent human reader catches wrong tone, odd wording and spelling. Word counts do not show meaning, and back-translation alone can miss problems.

quiz.question: AI adds a certificate to Bilal's CV that he does not have. Why is it important to remove it?
options: Certificates are not allowed on CVs in Pakistan
AI tools charge extra for adding certificates
Employers can check, and a false claim can cost him the job and his reputation
It makes the CV one line too long, and most employers in Pakistan reject any CV that goes over one page
quiz.explanation: Honesty matters on a CV. False claims can be found during checks or interviews and damage trust.

quiz.question: When summarising a long report with AI, what is a sensible way to avoid missing key points?
options: Summarise section by section and skim the original for anything missed
Ask for the shortest possible summary in one sentence
Only read the AI's summary and never open the original
Paste only the first page, as reports usually repeat themselves
quiz.explanation: Working section by section and comparing with the original reduces the chance of an important point being dropped.

quiz.question: Which task needs the strongest kind of check?
options: Ideas for a cousin's birthday message
A funny caption for a family photo
Three name ideas for a WhatsApp group
The correct dose of a medicine for an elderly relative
quiz.explanation: When a mistake could harm someone, use a doctor, pharmacist or official source. Low-stakes creative tasks need little checking.

quiz.question: How can you get help with a complaint reply without sharing a customer's private details?
options: Paste the customer's full details but ask the AI, politely and clearly, to keep them secret and forget them afterwards
Replace the name and order number with placeholders like [Customer] and [Order]
Send the customer's phone number so the AI can reply directly
Ask the customer to write the reply themselves
quiz.explanation: Placeholders keep the question useful while keeping personal data out of the tool. A promise from the tool is not a privacy control.

quiz.question: Ayesha's university says assignments must be students' own work. Which use of AI fits best?
options: Asking AI to write the assignment and changing a few words
Using AI to explain topics and create practice questions, then writing her own answers
Asking a friend to submit an AI answer under her name
Using AI to write the whole assignment, as long as she changes the font and no one at the university finds out
quiz.explanation: Learning support fits academic honesty. Submitting AI-written work as your own usually breaks the rules. Always check your own institution's policy.

quiz.question: An AI tool gives a confident price for a government fee. What should you do?
options: Trust it, because fees never change
Ask the same AI tool the same question again in a new chat and accept the second answer if it matches
Use the average of the AI's answer and a friend's guess
Check the current fee on the official government website or office
quiz.explanation: Fees change and AI may be out of date or wrong. Official sources are the only reliable check. Asking the same tool again is not independent proof.

sessions.title: Prompt Frameworks and Iterating Like a Professional
sessions.summary: Step up from one-off prompts to reusable briefs. Use a five-part framework, add examples, chaining, delimiters and stated assumptions, iterate one change at a time and build a prompt library you can rely on at work.
objectives: Write a five-part brief: role, goal, context and inputs, format and limits
Apply few-shot examples, chaining, delimiters and stated assumptions
Iterate a prompt one change at a time against a clear checklist
Build and maintain a versioned prompt library
Use self-review wisely without treating it as verification

cards.title: Same prompt, different day
cards.setting: A co-working space in Blue Area, Islamabad. Bilal now works as a junior analyst at a small logistics company and has joined Premium.

lines.text: My manager loved the weekly update I made with AI last month. This week I typed something similar and the result was weak. Why?
Did you type exactly the same thing?
No. I just wrote it quickly from memory. I did not save the good one.
That is the step up for Advanced. Beginners write a new prompt every time. Professionals build a brief they can reuse, test and improve.
Like a recipe? Same ingredients, same steps, so it tastes the same every time?
Exactly like a recipe. Today: a prompt framework, the tricks that make answers sharper, and a way of iterating that does not waste your time.

scenes.heading: Role
scenes.narration: Tell the tool what kind of helper to be. 'Act as an experienced operations analyst who writes clear updates for busy managers.' A role sets the vocabulary and the standard.

scenes.heading: Goal
scenes.narration: Say what the output is for. 'So my manager can decide in two minutes whether to add a second delivery van.' A goal helps the tool choose what matters.

scenes.heading: Context and inputs
scenes.narration: Give the facts it must use: this week's numbers, the audience, past decisions. Label them clearly, for example 'DATA:' followed by your table.

scenes.heading: Format
scenes.narration: Describe the shape: 'Three headings, no more than 150 words, one table, end with a recommendation.' Exact formats give consistent results.

scenes.heading: Limits
scenes.narration: Say what to avoid or never do. 'Use only the data I gave. If something is missing, say so instead of guessing.' Limits reduce invented facts.

cards.title: Role, Goal, Context, Format, Limits
cards.caption: A reusable structure for any serious prompt. Save the good ones.

items.label: Role
items.detail: Who the tool should act as.

items.label: Goal
items.detail: What the output is for and who will use it.

items.label: Context and inputs
items.detail: The facts, data and background it must use.

items.label: Format
items.detail: Length, sections, tables and tone.

items.label: Limits
items.detail: What to avoid, and what to do when information is missing.

cards.question: Which line from a brief is a 'Limit'?
options: 'Act as an experienced HR officer'
'Use only the figures in the DATA section; if a figure is missing, write MISSING'
'This is for a team meeting on Monday morning'
'Use three headings and one short table'
cards.explanation: A limit tells the tool what not to do and how to handle gaps. The others are role, goal and format.

cards.title: Techniques that sharpen answers
cards.body:
Once your brief is solid, these techniques lift quality further:

- **Give examples (few-shot):** show one or two samples of the output you want. The tool copies the pattern.
- **Break big tasks into steps (chaining):** outline first, then draft each section, then edit. Each step is easier to check.
- **Ask for options:** 'Give three different subject lines' lets you choose instead of accepting one.
- **Ask it to state assumptions:** 'List anything you assumed' exposes guesses.
- **Ask for a self-review:** 'Check your draft against my format and limits and fix any gaps.' Useful, but it does not replace your own check.
- **Use delimiters:** put pasted text between clear markers like ### so the tool knows where your data starts and ends.

cards.back: Show one to three examples of good output so the tool follows the same pattern and style.
Split a big job into smaller prompts: outline, then sections, then final edit. Check each step.
Mark pasted data with clear separators such as ### or triple quotes, so instructions and data do not mix.
Ask the tool to list guesses it made, so you can correct them before using the output.
Give the tool your checklist for a good answer and ask it to score its draft against it.
A saved, labelled collection of your best prompts, with notes on when to use each.

cards.title: The iteration loop
cards.caption: Improve one thing at a time, so you know what made the difference.

items.label: Run the brief
items.detail: Use your saved prompt with fresh inputs.

items.label: Judge against a checklist
items.detail: Accuracy, format, tone, length, missing points.

items.label: Change one thing
items.detail: Add a limit, an example or clearer context.

items.label: Save the better version
items.detail: Update your prompt library with a short note.

cards.title: The update keeps inventing numbers
cards.situation: Bilal's weekly update prompt sometimes includes delivery figures that were not in his data. His manager noticed one wrong number last week. What is the best fix?

choices.text: Add a limit: 'Use only the figures in DATA; write MISSING if needed', label the data clearly, and check every number before sending
choices.outcome: Best fix. Clear labels and a firm limit reduce invented figures, and his own check catches what slips through. The responsibility for numbers stays with him.

choices.text: Ask the tool to 'be more accurate' at the end of the prompt
choices.outcome: Vague. 'Be accurate' does not tell the tool how. A specific limit and labelled data work much better.

choices.text: Stop including any numbers in the update
choices.outcome: This avoids the risk but removes what the manager needs most. Fix the prompt and the checking instead.

choices.text: Switch to a different AI tool and keep the same prompt and process
choices.outcome: Any tool can invent figures. Without a better brief and a check, the problem can return.

cards.title: Match the problem to the technique
cards.prompt: Match each prompt problem to the technique that best fixes it.

pairs.left: The style never matches your company's reports
pairs.right: Give one or two examples of good past reports

pairs.left: A long report comes out messy and shallow
pairs.right: Break it into steps: outline, sections, then edit

pairs.left: The tool mixes your instructions with pasted text
pairs.right: Wrap the pasted text in clear delimiters

pairs.left: You cannot tell what the tool guessed
pairs.right: Ask it to list its assumptions

pairs.left: You keep losing your best prompts
pairs.right: Keep a labelled prompt library

cards.question: Why should you change only one thing at a time when improving a prompt?
options: Because AI tools reject prompts that change more than one line
Because each change costs a fixed fee on every plan
So you can tell which change actually improved the result
Because the first version is always the best one anyway
cards.explanation: Changing one thing at a time shows cause and effect. If you change five things, you cannot tell which one helped.

cards.title: Bilal's saved brief
cards.body:
Bilal's improved prompt, saved in his library as 'Weekly ops update v3':

> **Role:** You are an operations analyst writing for a busy general manager.
> **Goal:** Help the GM decide quickly if we need extra delivery capacity next week.
> **Inputs:** Weekly figures between ### marks below.
> **Format:** Headings: Summary, What changed, Risks, Recommendation. Max 180 words. One table of the five key figures.
> **Limits:** Use only figures from the inputs. Write MISSING for any gap. No jargon.
> ###
> [paste this week's figures here]
> ###

Note in his library: 'v3 added the MISSING rule after a wrong figure in week 6.'

cards.title: Build and refine a reusable prompt
cards.prompt: Put the steps for creating a reliable, reusable prompt in order.
steps: Write a first brief with role, goal, context, format and limits
Test it with real inputs and judge the result against a checklist
Change one element, such as adding an example or a limit
Test again with different inputs to see if it holds up
Save the best version with a version number and short note

cards.title: Ask the tool to improve your prompt
cards.body: A useful move: paste your prompt and ask 'What information is missing from this prompt for you to do the task well? Suggest an improved version.' You still decide what to keep, but it often spots gaps such as audience or length.

cards.question: Which use of a 'self-review' instruction is most sensible?
options: Use it to catch format gaps, then still check facts and figures yourself
Use it instead of any human check, because the tool has reviewed itself
Use it only for casual messages and never for work outputs
Use it to make the tool reveal its secret training data
cards.explanation: Self-review can improve structure and catch obvious gaps, but a tool checking itself is not independent verification of facts.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Workshop
items: Use a five-part brief: role, goal, context and inputs, format, and limits.
Examples, chaining, options, delimiters and stated assumptions make answers sharper and more consistent.
Iterate one change at a time and judge each version against a clear checklist.
Keep a prompt library with version numbers and notes on what changed and why.
Self-review helps with structure but never replaces your own check of facts and figures.

cards.prompt: Pick a task you do every week. Draft a five-part brief for it, and write the checklist you would use to judge the result. What one limit would protect you from the most likely mistake?

quiz.question: In the five-part brief, what does the 'Goal' describe?
options: What the output is for and who will use it
The kind of expert the tool should act as
The exact number of words in the reply
The data the tool must not use
quiz.explanation: The goal explains the purpose and audience, which helps the tool decide what matters. Role, format and limits are separate parts.

quiz.question: What is 'few-shot' prompting?
options: Asking a question with as few words as possible
Running the same prompt a few times in different chats and then picking one of the answers at random
Including one to three examples of the output you want in your prompt
Using AI only a few times a week to save money
quiz.explanation: Few-shot prompting shows the tool examples so it follows the same pattern and style.

quiz.question: Bilal splits a long report into outline, then sections, then a final edit. What is this technique called?
options: Delimiting
Few-shot prompting
Role setting
Chaining
quiz.explanation: Chaining breaks a big task into a series of smaller prompts, each easier to check and improve.

quiz.question: Why use delimiters such as ### around pasted text?
options: Because AI tools cannot read any pasted text at all unless it is surrounded by special symbols
So the tool can clearly separate your instructions from your data
To make the prompt look more professional to managers
To stop the tool from reading the pasted text at all
quiz.explanation: Clear markers show where pasted data starts and ends, reducing the chance that the tool confuses data with instructions.

quiz.question: Which limit best reduces invented figures in a report?
options: 'Be accurate and professional'
'Write the report as fast as you can'
'Use only the figures provided; write MISSING where data is absent'
'Make the numbers look impressive'
quiz.explanation: A specific rule about sources and gaps works better than a vague request. Your own check is still needed.

quiz.question: When iterating on a prompt, why change only one thing at a time?
options: To see clearly which change made the result better or worse
Because tools forget everything if you change two lines
Because longer prompts are always rejected
Because the tool needs time to rest between changes
quiz.explanation: Single changes show cause and effect, so you learn what works and can keep it.

quiz.question: What is the main benefit of a prompt library with version notes?
options: It makes every AI answer automatically correct
It lets you avoid checking outputs ever again
You can reuse proven prompts and remember why each change was made
It is required by law in most countries for anyone who uses AI tools at work for reports
quiz.explanation: A library brings consistency and learning over time. It does not remove the need to check outputs.

quiz.question: Ayesha asks the tool to 'list any assumptions you made'. Why is that useful?
options: It reveals guesses she can correct before using the output
It forces the tool to stop making any guesses in future chats
It deletes the tool's earlier mistakes from the conversation
It proves that the output is free of errors
quiz.explanation: Listing assumptions brings hidden guesses into view. It helps, but it does not prove the answer is correct.

quiz.question: After asking the tool to review its own draft against a checklist, what should you still do?
options: Nothing more, because a self-review by the tool guarantees that every fact and figure is accurate
Ask it to review again until it says 'perfect'
Send the draft immediately to save time
Check facts and figures yourself against the source data
quiz.explanation: A tool checking its own work is not independent verification. You remain responsible for facts and figures.

quiz.question: Which prompt line sets a 'Role'?
options: 'Use a table with three columns'
'Act as a patient tutor who explains accounting to first-year students'
'Do not mention any company names'
'This is for my exam revision next week'
quiz.explanation: A role tells the tool what kind of helper to be. The other lines are format, limit and goal.

sessions.title: AI for Work Outputs: Reports, Spreadsheets, Presentations and Images
sessions.summary: Use AI to speed up real work: outline and draft reports, get spreadsheet formulas you test before trusting, plan clear presentations and create images within the rules, with a verification routine for every number, claim and visual.
objectives: Outline and draft reports with AI from your own data and verify every figure
Request, understand and test spreadsheet formulas before applying them
Plan presentations with one message per slide and your own speaker notes
Use AI-generated images responsibly, checking terms and avoiding real people's likeness
Apply a verification routine to every AI-assisted work output

cards.title: The report that nearly went out
cards.setting: Bilal's office at the logistics company, Islamabad. Thursday, 5 p.m. The monthly report is due to the general manager tomorrow morning.

lines.text: AI wrote my monthly report in two minutes. It even says on-time deliveries rose by 12 percent. Looks great!
Where did 12 percent come from?
Let me check my spreadsheet... On-time deliveries went from 82 to 87 percent. That is 5 points, not 12.
I had the same thing with my sales sheet. The total in the AI summary did not match my own sum.
AI is a brilliant assistant for work outputs: reports, formulas, slides, even images. But every number and claim must be verified, because your name is on it.
Then teach me how to use it properly at work, with checks built in.

cards.title: AI across four kinds of work output

scenes.heading: Reports
scenes.narration: Ask for an outline first, then draft each section from your own data. Give the audience and the decision the report supports. Recalculate every figure yourself before it goes anywhere.

scenes.heading: Spreadsheet help
scenes.narration: Describe your columns and what you want, and ask for a formula with a plain explanation. Test it on a few rows where you know the answer, then apply it to the full sheet.

scenes.heading: Presentations
scenes.narration: Ask for a slide outline: one message per slide, a title, three short points and speaker notes. Some tools can build slides for you; features vary by tool and version.

scenes.heading: Images
scenes.narration: Image generators can create illustrations from text descriptions. Check the tool's terms on commercial use, avoid images of real people, and look closely for errors such as garbled text.

scenes.heading: Verification every time
scenes.narration: Numbers, names, sources, formulas and images all get checked before use. The faster the draft, the more careful the check.

cards.title: Verify before you present
cards.caption: A routine for any AI-assisted work output.

items.label: Trace every number
items.detail: Find it in your own data; recalculate totals and percentages.

items.label: Check names and facts
items.detail: Against company records or trusted sources.

items.label: Test formulas
items.detail: On a few rows where you already know the answer.

items.label: Inspect visuals
items.detail: Charts match the data; images have no errors or misleading content.

items.label: Read it as the audience
items.detail: Is it clear, fair and true? Would you defend each line?

cards.question: On-time deliveries went from 82 percent to 87 percent. How should Bilal describe this in his report?
options: An increase of 12 percentage points
An increase of 87 percent
An increase of 5 percentage points
A decrease of 5 percent
cards.explanation: 87 minus 82 is 5 percentage points. (As a relative change it is about 6 percent.) AI tools can mix these up, so recalculate yourself.

cards.title: Getting spreadsheet help you can trust
cards.body:
AI can explain and write formulas, but you must test them. A clear request names the columns and the result:

> My sheet has City in column A, Product in column B and Sales in column C, rows 2 to 200. Give me a formula for total sales in Lahore, and explain each part.

A typical answer is **=SUMIF(A2:A200,"Lahore",C2:C200)**: it checks column A for 'Lahore' and adds the matching values in column C.

- Test on a small range where you can add the numbers by hand.
- Check that the ranges cover all your rows.
- Some functions exist only in newer versions of Excel or in Google Sheets; if a formula gives an error, tell the tool which program and version you use.
- Never paste confidential data just to get a formula. Describe the columns instead.

cards.title: Formula to meaning
cards.prompt: Match each spreadsheet formula to what it does.

pairs.right: Adds all the values in cells C2 to C50
Finds the mean of the values in D2 to D31
Counts cells in B2 to B100 that contain 'Paid'
Adds values in column C where column A says 'Lahore'
Shows 'Target met' if E2 is 50,000 or more, otherwise 'Below'

cards.title: Weak vs professional AI use at work
cards.caption: The difference is rarely the tool. It is the process around it.

items.label: Report
items.left: Paste data, ask for a report, send it
items.right: Outline first, draft sections, recalculate every figure

items.label: Formula
items.left: Copy the first formula into the whole sheet
items.right: Test on known rows, check ranges, then apply

items.label: Slides
items.right: One message per slide, edited to your story and data

items.label: Images
items.left: Use any image for any purpose
items.right: Check terms and licence, avoid real people, inspect details

items.label: Data
items.right: Use approved tools, remove or describe sensitive data

cards.title: A generated image for Nasreen's sale poster
cards.situation: Nasreen wants a striking image for her Faisalabad boutique's sale poster. Her nephew suggests generating an image of a famous actress wearing one of Nasreen's suits. What should she do?

choices.text: Generate an original image of a model who is not a real person, check the tool's terms for commercial use, and inspect the image for errors
choices.outcome: Best choice. She avoids using a real person's likeness without permission, which can mislead customers and create legal trouble, and she checks she is allowed to use the image commercially.

choices.text: Generate the actress image, because it is AI-made and not a real photo
choices.outcome: Risky. Showing a real person appearing to endorse a product without permission can mislead customers and may break laws and platform rules, even if the image is generated.

choices.text: Skip images and use only text on the poster
choices.outcome: Safe, but she loses a useful option. Original generated images, used within the tool's terms, can work well.

cards.title: Ready, test first, or stop?
cards.prompt: Sort each AI work output by what you should do before using it.
buckets: Do not use as it is

items.text: A summary of your own meeting notes
A slide outline for a team presentation
A new formula for a 2,000-row sales sheet
A macro or script to rename files in a shared folder
A report figure you cannot find in your data
An image showing a real politician holding your product
A chart description that matches your recalculated totals
A quoted 'study' with no source you can find

cards.question: The AI suggests a formula that works in a newer spreadsheet version, but Bilal's office computer shows an error. What is the best next step?
options: Tell the tool which program and version he uses and ask for an alternative
Conclude that the data in his sheet must be wrong
Delete the column that causes the error
Ask colleagues to stop using the spreadsheet
cards.explanation: Functions differ between programs and versions. Giving the tool this context usually produces a formula that works for you.

cards.title: Nasreen's sales review deck
cards.body:
Fictional example. Nasreen meets a bank officer in Faisalabad about a small business loan and wants five clear slides.

1. She asks AI: 'Create an outline for 5 slides about my boutique's last 12 months: title, 3 short points and speaker notes for each. Audience: a bank loan officer.'
2. She fills in her real figures from her own records, not from the AI.
3. She recalculates the yearly total and the best month by hand.
4. She deletes one slide point the AI added about 'national market share', because she had no source for it.
5. She practises with the speaker notes, rewritten in her own words.

The officer asked two hard questions. She could answer both, because every number was hers.

cards.title: Build an AI-assisted report safely
cards.prompt: Put the steps for producing a work report with AI in order.
steps: Define the audience and the decision the report supports
Ask AI for an outline and adjust it to your needs
Provide your own data and draft each section
Recalculate every figure and check every claim
Edit for your voice, then share with a note on sources

cards.title: Describe the data instead of pasting it
cards.body: For formula and chart help, you rarely need real data. Describe the structure: 'Column A has dates, B has branch names, C has amounts.' Or make a few fake sample rows. You get the same help with no confidential information leaving your computer.

cards.question: Which statement about AI-generated images for business use is most accurate?
options: All AI images are free to use for any purpose in every country
AI images can never be used in business materials
Only images with no text in them need to be checked
Rules on commercial use vary by tool, so check its terms and avoid real people's likeness
cards.explanation: Terms of use differ between tools and can change. Using a real person's likeness without permission is risky. Inspect every image before use.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Office Tower
items: AI can speed up reports, formulas, slides and images, but every output needs verification before use.
Recalculate every figure yourself and know the difference between percentage points and percent change.
Test formulas on rows where you know the answer, and tell the tool your program and version.
For images, check the tool's terms for commercial use, avoid real people's likeness and inspect for errors.
Describe data structures or use fake samples instead of pasting confidential data.

cards.prompt: Think of a report, sheet or presentation you will produce in the next month. Where could AI help most, and which verification step would you add so you can defend every number?

quiz.question: What does =SUMIF(A2:A200,"Karachi",C2:C200) calculate?
options: The number of rows where column A says 'Karachi'
The total of column C values where column A says 'Karachi'
The average of column C for all cities except Karachi
The total of column A values where column C says 'Karachi'
quiz.explanation: SUMIF checks the first range for the condition and adds the matching values from the sum range, here column C.

quiz.question: Sales rose from 40 percent of target to 50 percent of target. What is the correct description?
options: A rise of 50 percent of target
A rise of 10 percent of total sales
A rise of 90 percentage points
A rise of 10 percentage points
quiz.explanation: 50 minus 40 is 10 percentage points. As a relative change that is 25 percent, which is a different measure.

quiz.question: Before applying an AI-suggested formula to 2,000 rows, what should you do?
options: Test it on a few rows where you already know the right answer
Apply it at once and fix any errors later in the month
Ask the AI whether the formula is correct for all 2,000 rows and accept its answer if it says yes
Delete the old formulas so there is no confusion
quiz.explanation: Testing on known rows shows whether the formula and ranges work before you trust it on the whole sheet.

quiz.question: A good AI slide outline usually has which feature?
options: As many points as possible on each slide
Full paragraphs copied from the report on every slide
One main message per slide with a few short points
Different fonts on each slide to keep people awake
quiz.explanation: One message per slide keeps the audience focused. Crowded slides are hard to follow.

quiz.question: Why is generating an image of a real celebrity 'using' your product a bad idea?
options: Because image tools cannot create faces of any kind
Because celebrities' images always look blurry
Because posters with people in them never sell well
It can mislead customers and may break laws and platform rules on likeness
quiz.explanation: Implying a real person endorses a product without permission is misleading and legally risky, even if the image is generated.

quiz.question: An AI-written report quotes a 'national study' with no source. What should Bilal do?
options: Keep it, because a national study makes the report sound well researched and managers like that
Remove the claim unless he can find and check the original source
Change the wording slightly so it is not a direct quote
Add a footnote saying 'source: AI'
quiz.explanation: Unverifiable claims should not go into work outputs. AI can invent studies that sound real.

quiz.question: How can you get formula help without sharing confidential sales data?
options: Paste the real file but delete the title row
Send the file to a personal e-mail first, then paste it
Describe the columns or use a few fake sample rows
Ask a colleague to paste it instead of you
quiz.explanation: The structure is usually all the tool needs. Fake samples or a description keep real data private.

quiz.question: A formula from AI gives an error on an older spreadsheet program. What is the likely reason?
options: The function may only exist in newer versions or a different program
Spreadsheets cannot use formulas written by AI
The computer needs to be restarted twice
The numbers in the sheet are too large to add
quiz.explanation: Function availability differs by program and version. Tell the tool what you use and ask for an alternative.

quiz.question: What is the first step in producing an AI-assisted report?
options: Ask the AI to write the full report from a single sentence, then fix the details later if anyone complains
Choose the colour scheme and fonts
Define the audience and the decision the report should support
Send the draft to your manager for checking
quiz.explanation: Knowing the audience and decision shapes the outline, the data and the recommendation.

quiz.question: What does =IF(E2>=50000,"Target met","Below") show when E2 is 49,999?
options: Below
Target met
An error message
quiz.explanation: 49,999 is less than 50,000, so the condition is false and the formula shows the second text, 'Below'.

sessions.title: Building Repeatable AI Workflows Responsibly
sessions.summary: Turn your best prompts into documented team workflows with inputs, checks, human approval and an issue log, and build in data privacy, fairness, copyright and company policy from the start so people can trust your AI work.
objectives: Choose suitable tasks for AI workflows using value and risk
Design a six-step workflow with inputs, prompt, draft, checks, approval and log
Protect data privacy with approved tools and anonymised inputs
Check outputs for bias and respect copyright and tool terms
Follow company policy and keep human accountability clear

cards.title: Ten hours a week, and one big worry
cards.setting: A meeting room at Bilal's logistics company, Islamabad. Bilal has been asked to share his AI methods with the team.

lines.text: My manager wants the whole team to use my weekly update method. He says it saves me two hours every week.
I want the same for my boutique: product descriptions, replies to customer questions, monthly summaries. Every week, the same way.
But what about privacy? And the job advert you made last month, Bilal. Didn't it say 'young energetic men preferred'?
It did. I removed it, but I almost did not notice.
This is the final stage. A repeatable workflow multiplies the good and the bad. So we build in privacy, fairness, copyright and company policy from the start.
Done well, you become the person your team trusts with AI. That is a real career skill.

cards.title: From one good prompt to a reliable workflow

scenes.heading: Pick the right task
scenes.narration: Choose work that repeats often, follows a pattern and is easy to check, such as weekly updates, product descriptions or meeting summaries. Avoid starting with high-risk decisions.

scenes.heading: Map the steps
scenes.narration: Write down inputs, the saved prompt, the output, the checks and who approves. A workflow is a recipe that someone else could follow.

scenes.heading: Build in protection
scenes.narration: Use only company-approved tools, remove personal data, add a fairness and accuracy checklist, and decide where a human must review.

scenes.heading: Test and measure
scenes.narration: Run it on several real examples. Note errors, time saved and fixes needed. Improve the prompt and checks, then try again.

scenes.heading: Document and share
scenes.narration: Write a one-page guide: purpose, steps, prompt, checklist, owner and date. Review it regularly, because tools and policies change.

cards.title: The six-step AI workflow
cards.caption: A simple design anyone on the team can follow and audit.

items.label: Inputs
items.detail: What goes in, from where, with sensitive data removed.

items.label: Saved prompt
items.detail: The tested brief, with a version number.

items.label: AI draft
items.detail: Produced in a company-approved tool.

items.label: Checks
items.detail: Accuracy, fairness, privacy and format checklist.

items.label: Human approval
items.detail: A named person reviews before anything goes out.

items.label: Log and improve
items.detail: Record issues and update the prompt or checklist.

cards.title: Which tasks to automate first?
cards.caption: Start in the top-left: high value and low risk. Treat high-risk tasks with strong human control.

items.label: High value, low risk
items.detail: Weekly internal updates, meeting summaries: good first workflows.

items.label: High value, high risk
items.detail: Customer-facing replies, hiring texts: allowed only with strong checks and human approval.

items.label: Low value, low risk
items.detail: Occasional fun posts: fine, but not worth a full workflow.

items.label: Low value, high risk
items.detail: Anything with sensitive personal data for little gain: do not automate.

cards.question: Which task is the best first candidate for a repeatable AI workflow?
options: Deciding which job applicants to reject
A weekly internal summary built from the team's own notes
Writing final medical advice for customers
Approving staff loans based on their salary slips
