cards.explanation: Start with frequent, low-risk, easy-to-check work. Decisions that affect people's jobs, health or money need strong human judgement and often legal controls.

cards.title: Four responsibilities that travel with every workflow
cards.body:
**1. Data privacy.** Use only tools your organisation has approved. Remove names, ID numbers and personal details unless policy allows them. Settings on how chats are stored or used for training vary by tool and plan, so check them and follow company rules.

**2. Bias and fairness.** AI learned from human text, including stereotypes. Check outputs for unfair assumptions about gender, age, religion, ethnicity, disability or region, especially in hiring, lending and customer service.

**3. Copyright.** Do not paste others' paid content to copy it, and do not present copied work as your own. Rules on owning and using AI outputs differ by country and by tool terms; get advice for important commercial use.

**4. Company policy and honesty.** Follow your employer's AI policy. Tell people when AI was used if policy or the situation requires it. A human stays accountable.

cards.title: Responsible AI words, in plain English

cards.back: When an output treats a group unfairly, often by repeating stereotypes found in the text the AI learned from.
Remove or replace details that identify a person, such as names, phone numbers and ID numbers.
A named person reviews and approves AI output before it is used or sent.
Your organisation's rules on which AI tools to use, for what, and with which data.
Legal rights over creative work. Copying or reusing others' work may need permission or a licence.
Being open that AI helped create something, when policy, the client or the situation requires it.

cards.title: The biased job advert
cards.situation: Bilal's workflow drafts job adverts. A new draft for a warehouse supervisor says 'ideal for young, energetic men under 30'. His manager is busy and says 'just post it'. What should Bilal do?

choices.text: Remove the age and gender wording, describe the real job requirements, add a fairness check to the workflow and explain the change to his manager
choices.outcome: Best choice. Job requirements should be about the work, not age or gender. Fixing the checklist stops the problem repeating, and a short explanation keeps the manager informed.

choices.text: Post it, because the AI wrote it and the manager approved
choices.outcome: The organisation is responsible for what it publishes, not the tool. Discriminatory wording can harm candidates, the company's reputation and may break employment rules.

choices.text: Remove the wording this time but change nothing else
choices.outcome: Good for this advert, but the workflow may repeat the same bias next time. Adding a fairness check fixes the cause.

cards.title: Which responsibility is at stake?
cards.prompt: Sort each situation by the main responsibility it raises.

items.text: Pasting a customer list with phone numbers into a personal AI account
An AI reply that assumes a customer from a village cannot use online banking
Copying a paid online course's text to rewrite it as your own training
Using an unapproved AI tool for confidential board papers
Uploading staff salary slips to get a summary
A product description that says 'perfect for housewives' for a laptop
Selling AI images without checking the tool's terms for commercial use
Including patients' names in a request to summarise clinic notes

cards.question: A colleague says, 'The AI made the mistake, so it is not our fault.' What is the professional response?
options: Agree, because AI companies are responsible for every output
The person and organisation using AI stay accountable for what they publish or send
Agree, as long as the mistake was in a customer e-mail
Blame the colleague who wrote the prompt and move on
cards.explanation: AI is a tool. Accountability stays with the people who choose to use its output, which is why human review and checks matter.

cards.title: Nasreen's product description workflow
cards.body:
Fictional example. Nasreen adds 30 new suits a month to her online shop. Her one-page workflow:

- **Inputs:** fabric, colours, sizes and care notes from her own stock sheet. No customer data.
- **Prompt:** saved brief 'Product text v4' with role, goal, format (title, 60-word description, care line) and limits ('no claims like best quality in Pakistan', 'no health claims').
- **Checks:** fabric and sizes match the stock sheet; no exaggerated or unfair wording; Urdu version read by her assistant.
- **Approval:** Nasreen reads each one before publishing.
- **Log:** a note column for problems found.

Time per product fell from 15 minutes to about 4, and errors are now caught before customers see them.

cards.title: Workflow part to purpose
cards.prompt: Match each part of an AI workflow to the job it does.

pairs.right: Keep personal and confidential data out of the AI tool
Give consistent results and record what changed
Catch stereotypes and unfair wording before publishing
Make a named person accountable for the final output
Track problems so the prompt and checks can be improved

cards.title: Roll out a team AI workflow
cards.prompt: Put the steps for introducing an AI workflow to your team in order.
steps: Check your company's AI policy and approved tools
Choose a frequent, low-risk task and map its steps
Build the prompt and the accuracy, privacy and fairness checks
Pilot it on real examples and measure errors and time saved
Document it in a one-page guide with an owner and review date
Train the team and review the workflow regularly

cards.title: When there is no AI policy yet
cards.body: Many small organisations have no written AI policy. Do not treat that as permission for anything. Ask your manager which tools are acceptable, keep personal and confidential data out, write down what you use AI for, and suggest a short policy. Being the person who raises this early builds trust.

cards.question: Which statement about copyright and AI outputs is most accurate?
options: Anything an AI produces is always free of any copyright questions
AI outputs can never be used in any commercial work
Copyright only matters for images and never for written text
Rules differ by country and tool terms, so check terms and get advice for important commercial use
cards.explanation: Copyright and ownership of AI outputs are still developing areas and differ by country and tool. Check terms and seek advice where the stakes are high.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Control Room
items: Turn repeated, low-risk, easy-to-check tasks into documented workflows: inputs, prompt, draft, checks, approval, log.
Use only approved tools, anonymise data and check each tool's data settings against company policy.
Check every workflow output for bias, especially in hiring, lending and customer service.
Respect copyright and tool terms, and disclose AI use where policy or the situation requires it.
A named human stays accountable; the AI is never the excuse.

cards.prompt: Design one AI workflow for your study, job or business. Write its six steps, name the biggest privacy, bias or copyright risk, and the check that would catch it.

quiz.question: Which task suits a first repeatable AI workflow best?
options: Final decisions on which customers get loans
Diagnosing illnesses from patients' descriptions
Choosing which staff members to dismiss
Weekly summaries of the team's own meeting notes
quiz.explanation: Good first workflows are frequent, low risk and easy to check. Decisions about money, health and jobs need strong human judgement.

quiz.question: What does 'anonymise' mean when preparing inputs for AI?
options: Translate the text into another language first
Remove or replace details that identify a person
Delete all numbers from the document
Use the AI tool without creating an account
quiz.explanation: Anonymising means removing names, ID numbers, phone numbers and similar details so people cannot be identified.

quiz.question: An AI-drafted job advert says 'young men preferred'. What responsibility does this mainly raise?
options: Copyright
Bias and fairness
File storage
Spreadsheet accuracy
quiz.explanation: Requirements based on age or gender rather than the work are unfair and can break employment rules. A fairness check should catch them.

quiz.question: What is 'human in the loop'?
options: A person employed by the AI company who reads and types replies on its behalf during busy hours
A customer who complains about an AI reply
A group chat where people share AI answers
A named person reviews and approves AI output before it is used
quiz.explanation: Human review keeps accountability with people and catches errors before they reach others.

quiz.question: Your small company has no written AI policy. What is the best approach?
options: Ask your manager which tools are acceptable and keep confidential data out
Use any tool with any data, since nothing is forbidden
Stop using AI completely and tell nobody
Create a personal account and upload all company files
quiz.explanation: No policy is not permission. Ask, protect data, record your use and suggest a short policy.

quiz.question: Why should a workflow include an issue log?
options: So the AI tool can read the log each morning and fix its own mistakes automatically without help
Because logs make the workflow run faster
So problems are recorded and the prompt and checks can be improved
So the team can blame whoever made each mistake
quiz.explanation: A log turns mistakes into improvements to the prompt and checklist.

quiz.question: Where should you check how a tool stores your chats or uses them to improve its models?
options: Nowhere, because all AI tools handle stored chats and training data in exactly the same way everywhere
In a social media post about the tool
By asking the AI in a chat, then relying on its answer
In the tool's privacy settings and terms, and against your company's policy
quiz.explanation: Data settings vary by tool and plan and can change. Read the official settings and terms, and follow company rules.

quiz.question: A colleague copies a paid online course's text into AI to 'rewrite it as our own training'. What is the main concern?
options: The text may be too long for the AI tool
Copyright and honesty about others' work
The AI might translate it into Urdu by mistake
Training materials do not need to be original
quiz.explanation: Reworking someone else's paid content to present as your own raises copyright and honesty problems, whatever tool is used.

quiz.question: Which is the correct order for the first steps of rolling out a team workflow?
options: Train the whole team, then check whether the tool is allowed
Document the workflow, then decide which task it is for
Check policy and approved tools, then choose a low-risk task and map its steps
Pilot with customer data, then check the company policy
quiz.explanation: Policy comes first, so the workflow is built on approved tools and rules. Then pick and map a suitable task.

quiz.question: A customer complains about a wrong AI-drafted reply. Who is accountable?
options: The business that chose to send the reply
The AI tool, because it wrote the text
The customer, for asking an unclear question
Nobody, because AI mistakes are nobody's fault
quiz.explanation: The organisation using the output is responsible for what it sends. That is why approval and checks are built into workflows.

bank.question: A friend says an AI tool must be right because it answered instantly and in perfect English. What is the best reply?
options: That is correct, as well-known AI tools are tested to make sure they never make factual mistakes
Only answers in Urdu can be wrong; English answers are checked
Speed and fluency show how it writes, not whether the facts are true
AI tools are right only when they answer slowly
bank.explanation: AI tools produce fluent text from patterns. Fluency is not evidence of accuracy, so important facts still need checking.

bank.question: Ayesha asks an AI tool for three books on Pakistani history. One title cannot be found anywhere. What most likely happened?
options: The tool generated a plausible but invented title, a hallucination
The book is rare and secret, and only AI tools with special library access know that it exists
The library website is broken and needs updating
Ayesha typed the question in the wrong language
bank.explanation: AI tools can invent references that sound real. Always confirm books, articles and quotes in a library catalogue or trusted source.

bank.question: Which task is better done with a search engine or official website than with an AI chat tool alone?
options: Rewording your own thank-you message to sound warmer
Getting ideas for a short speech at a family event
Explaining a maths concept you are revising
Finding the current admission deadline of a university
bank.explanation: Current deadlines change and must come from the official source. AI is well suited to rewording and explaining.

bank.question: Kamran is offered a 'premium AI app' through a link from an unknown number. Which sign most strongly suggests a scam?
options: The app has a colourful logo and a friendly name
It asks for payment to a personal mobile wallet and his OTP code
The message is written in Roman Urdu
It says the app can help with writing
bank.explanation: Requests for wallet payments to personal numbers and OTP codes are classic fraud signs. Use only official websites and verified app listings.

bank.question: Why is it misleading to say 'ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot and Claude all include the same features on their free plans'?
options: None of these tools offers any free use at all
Features and plans differ by tool, country and time, so they must be checked
They are all the same product sold under different names, so their plans are always identical
Free plans are fixed by law and never change
bank.explanation: Each tool sets its own plans, which vary and change. The safe habit is to check the current terms on the official site.

bank.question: In a new chat, Bilal types 'make it shorter' and the tool seems confused. Why?
options: The tool cannot shorten text in any situation
He must type the request in capital letters
Shortening only works for messages in Urdu
A new chat usually does not see the earlier conversation
bank.explanation: Chat history gives context for follow-ups. A fresh chat often starts without it, unless a memory feature is switched on.

bank.question: Which description of an AI chat assistant is most accurate for a beginner?
options: A fast helper that drafts and explains, whose work you check and decide on
A perfect expert whose advice can safely replace doctors, lawyers and teachers for most everyday decisions
A search engine that only lists links to websites
A human operator typing replies very quickly
bank.explanation: AI assistants generate drafts and explanations. They are not infallible experts, simple link lists or hidden humans.

bank.question: Which prompt best combines task, context, details and format?
options: 'Write replies'
'I have a bakery in Lahore and customers'
'Write 3 polite WhatsApp replies for my Lahore bakery to customers asking about delivery, under 40 words each'
'Make WhatsApp messages polite and short please'
bank.explanation: The best prompt has a task (write replies), context (Lahore bakery, delivery questions), details (polite, under 40 words) and format (3 replies).

bank.question: Bilal wants AI to write his CV summary but keeps getting generic text. Which instruction will help most?
options: 'Write an excellent, impressive CV summary that would suit anyone applying for any job in any industry'
'Make it sound very impressive'
'Use the word dynamic at least twice'
'Ask me five questions about my studies and experience before you write'
bank.explanation: Letting the tool ask questions first gives it real facts to work with, so it does not invent or stay generic.

bank.question: Ayesha's prompt is in Roman Urdu, but the reply comes in formal English that her mother cannot read. What should she have included?
options: A request for more emojis in the reply
The language and script she wanted for the reply
Her full name and date of birth
A request to search the internet first
bank.explanation: Stating the reply language and script, such as 'reply in Urdu script', avoids this. Personal details are not needed.

bank.question: A conversation has drifted badly after many messages. Which action is usually most efficient?
options: Keep correcting each small error message by message
Repeat the original vague prompt several more times
Start a new chat with one clear prompt containing all key details
Ask the tool to apologise for the confusion and then continue the same long conversation as before
bank.explanation: A fresh chat with a complete prompt removes the confusing history and often gets a good answer faster.

bank.question: Nasreen likes the style of one caption she wrote last year. What is the most effective way to get similar new captions?
options: Paste that caption as an example and ask for new ones in a similar style
Describe her style in one word, such as 'nice'
Ask for captions in 'the best style possible'
Ask the tool to guess her personal writing style from her shop's name and the city where it is located
bank.explanation: An example communicates tone, length and style much more clearly than a vague description.

bank.question: Which follow-up best fixes an answer that is accurate but far too long for a WhatsApp message?
options: 'This is wrong, try again'
'Add more information'
'Rewrite this in under 50 words, keeping the key details'
'Translate this into a different language'
bank.explanation: A clear length limit with an instruction to keep key details solves the actual problem. 'Wrong' gives no direction.

bank.question: In the prompt 'As a friendly tutor, explain fractions to my 10-year-old using pizza slices, in 5 short steps', which part is the format?
options: 'in 5 short steps'
'As a friendly tutor'
'explain fractions'
'to my 10-year-old'
bank.explanation: The format describes the shape of the answer. 'Friendly tutor' sets a role, 'explain fractions' is the task and 'my 10-year-old' is context.

bank.question: Nasreen asks AI to write to a supplier confirming '500 metres at Rs 450 per metre'. The draft says Rs 540. What does this show?
options: The supplier's price must have changed overnight, and the AI tool found out from the internet
AI tools always round prices upwards on purpose
She should stop writing prices in any e-mail
Every number in an AI draft must be checked against her own records
bank.explanation: AI can swap or invent digits. Checking numbers against your own records before sending is essential.

bank.question: Which approach to personalised customer messages protects privacy best?
options: Pasting names only, since names alone are never personal data
Templates with placeholders, filled in from her own list outside the AI tool
Pasting the full customer list but asking the tool to delete it from its memory as soon as it has finished
Pasting phone numbers only, since names are the sensitive part
bank.explanation: Placeholders give the benefit without sharing any customer data. A tool's promise to forget is not a privacy control.

bank.question: Which task belongs in the 'matters a lot and hard to check' corner, needing an official or professional source?
options: A caption for a cousin's wedding photo
Whether a medicine is safe to take with another medicine
A polite reminder to a friend about a loan
A summary of your own class notes
bank.explanation: Medicine interactions can cause harm and are hard for a non-expert to check, so ask a doctor or pharmacist.

bank.question: Ayesha must translate her degree transcript into English for a foreign university. What is the most responsible plan?
options: Submit the AI translation, as transcripts are simple documents
Ask AI to improve her grades in the translation
Translate only the grades and leave the rest out
Use AI to understand it, then follow the university's rules, which may require an official translation
bank.explanation: Official uses often require certified translations. AI can help understanding, but she must meet the institution's exact requirements and keep it truthful.

bank.question: AI rewrote Bilal's CV and added 'led a team of ten'. He once helped organise a university event with ten volunteers. What is the honest fix?
options: Describe what he actually did, such as 'helped organise a university event with ten volunteers'
Keep 'led a team of ten', because it is close enough
Remove the event, since volunteering never counts on a CV
Change it to 'managed a department' to sound more senior
bank.explanation: Honest, specific wording shows real experience without overstating it. Exaggerations can unravel in interviews or reference checks.

bank.question: Ayesha asks AI to summarise a 30-page report and gets a neat summary. What is the main remaining risk?
options: The summary will be longer than the report
The summary will always be in a different language
Important points may be missed or slightly changed, so she should compare with the original
The report will be deleted from her computer
bank.explanation: Summaries can drop or distort details. Skimming the original, especially headings and conclusions, catches gaps.

bank.question: Which use of AI best fits a university rule that assessed work must be the student's own?
options: Having AI write the essay and then running it through a rewording tool so the wording looks like her own
Writing the first line herself and letting AI write the rest
Using AI only for the conclusion, which is less important
Asking for practice questions and explanations, then writing her own answers
bank.explanation: Using AI to learn and practise supports academic honesty. Having AI write assessed work, even partly, usually breaks such rules; check the institution's policy.

bank.question: Which element of a five-part brief most directly reduces invented facts?
options: Role, such as 'act as a senior analyst'
Limits, such as 'use only the data provided and write MISSING for gaps'
Format, such as 'use three headings'
Goal, such as 'for a Monday meeting'
bank.explanation: Limits set rules about sources and gaps. Role, goal and format improve relevance and shape but do not control invention as directly.

bank.question: Bilal's report style never matches his company's past reports. Which technique should he try first?
options: Ask the tool to use 'the company style' without explaining it
Use more capital letters in his prompt
Include one or two short examples of past reports as a model
Split the report into ten separate chats
bank.explanation: Few-shot examples show the exact pattern and style wanted. The tool cannot know an unexplained company style.

bank.question: Why can chaining (outline, then sections, then edit) produce a better long document than one big prompt?
options: Each smaller step is easier to direct and to check before moving on
Chaining makes the tool switch to a more powerful model automatically, which gives better writing
Long prompts are always rejected by every AI tool
Chaining removes the need to check the final document
bank.explanation: Breaking the work up gives you control points. It does not change the model or remove the need to check.

bank.question: Bilal changed the role, format, limits and examples all at once, and the result got worse. What should he learn from this?
options: Never change a prompt once it has been written
Always use the longest prompt possible
Change one element at a time so he can see what caused the change
Switch to a new tool whenever results get worse
bank.explanation: With many changes at once, cause and effect is lost. Testing one change at a time shows what helps.

bank.question: What is the main purpose of putting pasted data between ### markers?
options: To separate the data clearly from the instructions
To hide the data from the AI tool
To make the AI reply in a table
To encrypt the data before sending it
bank.explanation: Delimiters show where the data starts and ends. They do not hide or protect data, so privacy rules still apply.

bank.question: Bilal asks the tool to review its draft against his checklist. It says 'All checks passed.' What should he do next?
options: Send it straight away, because the tool has checked its own draft and confirmed that it is correct
Ask for a second review and send it if it agrees
Delete the checklist, since it is no longer needed
Still check the facts and figures himself against his data
bank.explanation: Self-review is not independent verification. A tool can confidently confirm its own errors.

bank.question: Which note in a prompt library is most useful?
options: 'Good prompt'
'v3: added MISSING rule after a wrong figure in week 6; use for weekly ops update'
'Prompt from Tuesday'
'Use sometimes'
bank.explanation: A version number, the reason for the change and when to use it help anyone reuse and improve the prompt.

bank.question: A monthly report says customer complaints 'fell from 20 percent to 15 percent of orders, a 5 percent drop'. What is the precise wording?
options: A drop of 5 percent, which is the same thing as a fall of 5 percentage points in this situation
A drop of 5 percentage points, which is a 25 percent relative fall
A drop of 15 percentage points from the earlier level
A rise of 25 percent in complaints per order
bank.explanation: 20 to 15 is 5 percentage points. As a share of the starting 20, that is a 25 percent relative fall.

bank.question: Which formula correctly counts how many cells in B2:B300 contain the word 'Late'?
options: =SUM(B2:B300,"Late")
=COUNT("Late",B2:B300,TRUE)
=SUMIF("Late",B2:B300)
=COUNTIF(B2:B300,"Late")
bank.explanation: COUNTIF takes the range first and then the condition. SUM and COUNT do not take a text condition this way.

bank.question: An AI-suggested formula gives correct totals for rows 2 to 50 but the sheet has 400 rows. What is the most likely problem?
options: The formula's range stops at row 50 and misses the remaining rows
The formula only works on weekdays
Spreadsheets cannot add more than 50 numbers
The AI deliberately hid the other rows
bank.explanation: Check that ranges cover all your data. A short range gives totals that look right but leave rows out.

bank.question: Which is the strongest way to verify an AI-written monthly report before sending it?
options: Read it once quickly to make sure the tone sounds professional and the headings are in the right order
Ask the AI to confirm that all of its figures are correct
Trace every figure to the source data and recalculate totals and percentages
Check only the first and last paragraphs for errors
bank.explanation: Tracing and recalculating figures is independent verification. Tone checks and the tool's self-confirmation do not catch wrong numbers.

bank.question: Nasreen wants an AI image for her sale poster. Which plan is most responsible?
options: An image of a famous cricketer appearing to wear her suits
A copy of a rival shop's poster with her logo added
Any image, since generated images have no rules
An original image with no real person, used within the tool's terms and checked for errors
bank.explanation: Avoid real people's likeness and others' designs, check the tool's terms for commercial use and inspect for errors.

bank.question: AI produced a 20-slide deck for a 10-minute talk to a bank officer. What is the best edit?
options: Keep all 20 slides as the AI made them, and speak much faster so that everything fits into ten minutes
Cut to a few slides with one message each and replace figures with her own checked data
Add more text to each slide so nothing is missed
Present the slides exactly as the AI produced them
bank.explanation: Short, focused slides suit a short talk, and only her own verified figures should appear.

bank.question: Bilal needs help writing a formula but his sales file is confidential. What should he do?
options: Paste the confidential file into a personal AI account at home, where the company's rules do not apply
Paste half the file, since that is less risky
Describe the column layout or create a few fake rows and ask for the formula
E-mail the file to the AI company's support team
bank.explanation: Formula help needs the structure, not the real data. Describing columns or using fake samples keeps confidential data safe.

bank.question: Using a value and risk matrix, which task should NOT be automated?
options: Summarising patients' private records for a small gain in speed
Weekly internal meeting summaries from the team's notes
Drafting product descriptions from the stock sheet
Suggesting headings for an internal newsletter
bank.explanation: Low value and high risk, especially with sensitive personal data, should not be automated. The others are lower risk and easy to check.

bank.question: An AI customer reply says 'as a lady you may find our online app confusing, so visit a branch'. Which check should have caught this?
options: A spelling check on the customer's name
A check that the reply was under 100 words
A fairness check for stereotypes about gender and other groups
A check of the tool's subscription status
bank.explanation: This is a gender stereotype. A fairness checklist in the workflow catches assumptions like this before replies go out.

bank.question: Which workflow design best keeps accountability clear?
options: A named person approves each output, and issues are recorded in a log
The AI sends all outputs directly to customers, and the whole team reviews a sample of them once a year
Anyone may edit the prompt at any time without notes
Outputs go out automatically if they are under 100 words
bank.explanation: Named approval and an issue log show who is responsible and how problems are fixed.

bank.question: A colleague wants to upload confidential board papers to an AI tool the company has not approved, 'just to save time'. What is the best response?
options: Agree, as long as the board papers are deleted from the chat history straight after the summary is made
Agree, but upload them from a home computer
Agree, because AI companies never look at any uploaded file
Explain that company policy requires approved tools, and suggest an approved option or a manual summary
bank.explanation: Unapproved tools with confidential data break policy and create risk. Deleting afterwards or using another computer does not fix that.

bank.question: Which statement about copyright and AI is most responsible for a small business?
options: AI-created content is always fully owned by whoever typed the prompt, in every country and under every tool's terms
Check each tool's terms and get advice when AI content is central to a commercial product
Copyright never applies to text, only to music and films
Paid content can be reused freely once AI rewrites it
bank.explanation: Ownership and use of AI outputs vary by country and tool terms, and rewording others' work does not remove copyright concerns.

bank.question: Nasreen's product workflow has run well for months. What is a good reason to review it now?
options: Workflows stop working automatically after three months, and the AI tool must be reinstalled each time
Tools, terms and policies change, so the prompt and checks should be reviewed regularly
Reviewing is only needed when a customer complains
The AI tool needs to be told it is doing well
bank.explanation: Tools update, terms and laws change and new risks appear. A regular review date keeps the workflow safe and useful.

bank.question: Which is the best first step before rolling out an AI workflow to a team?
options: Train everyone on the workflow before checking anything
Pilot it on real customer data to see what happens
Write the final guide before the workflow is tested
Confirm the company's AI policy and which tools are approved
bank.explanation: Policy and approved tools come first, so the workflow is built within the rules. Testing and documentation follow.
